topic: Common atmospheric pollutants and their sources
subject: chemistry

items.q: Air above a busy city contains carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and particulates. What do these three pollutants have in common?
items.correct: They are all released by the combustion of fuels
items.misconception: They are all gases formed by incomplete combustion
items.why: Both are products of incomplete combustion and both are described using the word carbon, so the two are stored as one idea. Carbon monoxide is a gas, made of carbon and oxygen. Soot is solid carbon particles, with no oxygen in it, and it contributes to particulates in the atmosphere rather than acting as a toxic gas.
items.random_wrong: They are all produced from sulfur impurities in fuels

items.q: Which statement best describes the composition of most fuels?
items.correct: They contain carbon and/or hydrogen and may contain sulfur
items.misconception: They contain carbon and/or hydrogen and always contain sulfur
items.why: Sulfur dioxide appears in every list of combustion pollutants, so students read the list as things that always come out rather than things that may come out. The specification says most fuels contain carbon and/or hydrogen and may also contain some sulfur. Sulfur is an impurity in some fuels, such as coal. If a question tells you the fuel is sulfur-free, no sulfur dioxide can form.
items.random_wrong: They contain carbon and nitrogen and may also contain sulfur

items.q: A hydrocarbon fuel that contains no sulfur is burned in a plentiful supply of air. Which substances are released?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide and water vapour only
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide only
items.why: Water is thought of as the opposite of burning, so students resist listing it as something combustion makes. Hydrogen in the fuel is oxidised to water, which leaves as water vapour because the gases are hot. The specification lists water vapour among the gases released when a fuel is burned.
items.random_wrong: Carbon dioxide, water vapour, sulfur dioxide

items.q: Carbon monoxide is found in the exhaust gases of a petrol engine. Why is it produced?
items.correct: The oxygen supply is too small for the fuel to burn completely
items.misconception: The fuel contains impurities that cannot be burned fully in air
items.why: The word incomplete is read as a fault in the fuel, and soot looks like dirt, which reinforces the idea. Incomplete combustion is about the conditions, not the purity of the fuel. A perfectly pure hydrocarbon burns incompletely if there is not enough oxygen, producing carbon monoxide and carbon particles.
items.random_wrong: The carbon in the fuel reacts with nitrogen from the hot air

items.q: Oxides of nitrogen are formed inside a car engine. Where does the nitrogen come from, and why does it react?
items.correct: From the air, because the high temperature makes it react with oxygen
items.misconception: From nitrogen compounds in the fuel, which are oxidised as it burns
items.why: Students learn that the carbon in carbon dioxide and the sulfur in sulfur dioxide both come from the fuel, and generalise the pattern to every pollutant. Air is about four-fifths nitrogen, and the engine draws air in as well as fuel. At the high temperature inside the engine that nitrogen reacts with oxygen. Oxides of nitrogen are the one pollutant here that does not come from the fuel.
items.random_wrong: From the fuel, because incomplete combustion releases it from the fuel

items.q: A power station burns coal that contains a small amount of sulfur. How is sulfur dioxide produced?
items.correct: The sulfur in the coal is oxidised to sulfur dioxide as the coal burns
items.misconception: The coal burns incompletely, so sulfur dioxide escapes from the coal
items.why: Incomplete combustion is taught as the cause of the pollutants carbon monoxide and soot, and the rule is then over-extended to every pollutant. More oxygen cannot help here, because sulfur dioxide is already the oxidised product. The only way to avoid it is to remove the sulfur from the fuel or the sulfur dioxide from the waste gases.
items.random_wrong: Sulfur in the air is oxidised at the high temperature of the furnace

items.q: Black soot is deposited around the burner of a poorly adjusted gas heater. What is soot, and how has it formed?
items.correct: Solid carbon particles, formed by burning in too little oxygen
items.misconception: A colourless gas, formed by burning in too little oxygen
items.why: Both are products of incomplete combustion and both are described using the word carbon, so the two are stored as one idea. Carbon monoxide is a gas, made of carbon and oxygen. Soot is solid carbon particles, with no oxygen in it, and it contributes to particulates in the atmosphere rather than acting as a toxic gas.
items.random_wrong: Solid carbon particles, formed when carbon reacts with nitrogen

items.q: A fuel oil contains carbon, hydrogen and a small amount of sulfur. It is burned in a plentiful supply of air. Which products are formed?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide, water vapour and sulfur dioxide
items.misconception: Carbon monoxide, water vapour and sulfur dioxide
items.why: Students picture combustion as a sequence of steps rather than as one reaction whose products depend on how much oxygen is available. In a plentiful supply of oxygen the carbon is fully oxidised and carbon dioxide is the carbon-containing product. Carbon monoxide is a sign that the oxygen supply was limited.
items.random_wrong: Carbon dioxide, water vapour and carbon particles

items.q: Coke is a fuel that is almost pure carbon. A sample is burned in a limited supply of air. Which products would you expect?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and carbon particles
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide and water vapour
items.why: The complete combustion of hydrocarbons is practised so often that the pair carbon dioxide and water becomes an automatic answer for every fuel. Water can only form if the fuel contains hydrogen. Coke is almost pure carbon, so no water vapour is produced. Always check which elements the fuel contains before listing the products.
items.random_wrong: Carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide and carbon particles

items.q: An engine burns sulfur-free petrol in a plentiful supply of air. Which pollutant is still likely to be released, and where does it come from?
items.correct: Oxides of nitrogen, from the air drawn into the engine
items.misconception: Sulfur dioxide, from the sulfur present in the petrol
items.why: Sulfur dioxide appears in every list of combustion pollutants, so students read the list as things that always come out rather than things that may come out. The specification says most fuels contain carbon and/or hydrogen and may also contain some sulfur. Sulfur is an impurity in some fuels, such as coal. If a question tells you the fuel is sulfur-free, no sulfur dioxide can form.
items.random_wrong: Carbon monoxide, from the carbon in the petrol

items.q: Homes with gas boilers are advised to fit a carbon monoxide alarm. Why can people not rely on their own senses instead?
items.correct: It has no colour and no smell, so it is not easily detected
items.misconception: It has a faint smell that most people do not recognise
items.why: Students associate dangerous gases with a smell or a visible haze, because that is true of many gases they meet in a laboratory, such as chlorine and bromine. Carbon monoxide has no colour and no smell. That is exactly why it is so hazardous: there is no warning that it is present.
items.random_wrong: It is a solid particulate, so it settles out of the air

items.q: Which pair of pollutants released by burning fuels causes acid rain?
items.correct: Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
items.misconception: Carbon monoxide and oxides of nitrogen
items.why: Pollutants are learned as a single list rather than as separate substances with separate effects, so one effect is attached to all of them. Each pollutant has its own named effect. Carbon monoxide is toxic; particulates cause global dimming and health problems; only sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen are named as causes of acid rain.

items.q: Air beside a busy road contains sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen. What harm do these gases do to people who breathe them in?
items.correct: They cause respiratory problems in humans
items.misconception: They are harmless unless dissolved in rain
items.why: Carbon dioxide is the pollutant students hear about most, and they carry it across from the previous topic on the greenhouse effect into every question about environmental damage. In this specification acid rain is caused by sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen. Carbon dioxide is dealt with separately, as a greenhouse gas.
items.random_wrong: They are toxic but cannot be detected at all

items.q: Which two effects does the specification link to particulates in the atmosphere?
items.correct: Global dimming and health problems for humans
items.misconception: Acid rain and health problems for humans
items.why: Pollutants are learned as a single list rather than as separate substances with separate effects, so one effect is attached to all of them. Each pollutant has its own named effect. Carbon monoxide is toxic; particulates cause global dimming and health problems; only sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen are named as causes of acid rain.
items.random_wrong: Global warming and health problems for humans

items.correct: Less sunlight reaches the Earth's surface
items.misconception: The Sun gives out less light than before
items.why: The word global attaches to the Sun rather than to the atmosphere, and dimming sounds like a change in the source of the light. The Sun is unchanged. Particulates in the atmosphere are what reduce the sunlight reaching the surface, which is why global dimming is worst where fuels are burned heavily.
items.random_wrong: The average temperature of the Earth rises

items.q: A diesel engine releases solid carbon particles and unburned hydrocarbons. What do these form in the atmosphere, and what do they cause?
items.misconception: Acid rain, which damages trees and lakes
items.why: Pollutants are learned as a single list rather than as separate substances with separate effects, so one effect is attached to all of them. Each pollutant has its own named effect. Carbon monoxide is toxic; particulates cause global dimming and health problems; only sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen are named as causes of acid rain.
items.random_wrong: Carbon dioxide, which causes global warming

items.correct: Global dimming, and health problems for humans.
items.misconception: Particulates make the Earth warmer, because everything that comes out of a chimney adds to global warming.
items.why: Every pollution effect gets collapsed into one heading, global warming, so the specific effect named for particulates is lost. Particulates cause global dimming, which means less sunlight reaches the Earth's surface. They also cause health problems for humans.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How can unburned hydrocarbons contribute to particulates?
items.correct: They are released along with solid particles and form particulates in the atmosphere.
items.misconception: Unburned hydrocarbons are fuel vapour, so they are gases and cannot be part of particulates.
items.why: Particulate is taken to mean solid only, so anything that leaves the engine as a vapour is ruled out. The specification states that solid particles and unburned hydrocarbons may be released and that these form particulates in the atmosphere. Both are named as sources of particulates.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.9.3 Common atmospheric pollutants and their sources
